Marjorie Kettell  

The major premise of this book is that the intimate relationship between patient and analyst goes beyond classical transferences because of the development of a positive new experience. This new experience is an opportunity to reexperience the patient's past in the presence of a different person, the analyst, who reacts in ways that can promote growth of the patient's self and his/her self-in-relation-to-others.

The emphasis is on “the importance and value of positive new experience in the clinical situation” (p. 1). The authors have based their approach on a model they propose as an integration of self-psychology, attachment theory, infant research, trauma studies, developmental systems research, and brain research. The goal of analysis is “the self coming into being as a consolidated self” and connecting with the analyst as “an intimate other” with whom the patient feels safe and comfortable. Their assumption is that “given an adequate constitutional endowment, self and self-with-other consolidation will emerge” (p. 3).

The authors describe two key elements in the styles of interaction which promote intrapersonal and interpersonal growth.

As storied or narrative constructs, reporting of dreams becomes a unique mode of communication about the way in which the mind attempts to adapt to emotionally charged triggering events.

In contrast to obligatory or frank perverse sexuality, the term perverse defenses refers to certain modes of warding off intolerable affects, inner conflicts, external reality, and the experience of psychological “deadness.” Perverse defenses may involve seeking excited or altered states, taking risks, and engaging in sadomasochistic behavior, and they serve to avoid deeply felt commitment in a valued relationship. These defenses can markedly impede analytic process and may lead to treatment stalemate. Although patients with perverse defenses can profoundly challenge the treatment process and cause discouragement in the analyst, eventually they can achieve substantial analytic gain.

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall  

Arnold William Rachman, who is arguably the preeminent American Ferenczi scholar, has generated a study of Ferenczi that deserves reading by every student and practitioner of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis. Freud himself asserted that every psychoanalyst should remain a student of Ferenczi.

Rachman, a fourth generation analysand of Ferenczi (through Clara Thompson, Louis Wolberg, and Betty Feldman), has devoted the last twenty years to researching Ferenczi's life and work. This book is a well-written distillation of over fifty papers and presentations by Rachman. He covers not only Ferenczi's theories and techniques, but demonstrates how Ferenczi developed as a person and an analyst.

As an inquiring psychoanalyst, Rachman devotes considerable time to describing Ferenczi's early sociocultural environment, personal and family history and to dovetailing it with his development as student and physician. Ferenczi's complex relationship with Freud is spelled out in fascinating detail, from the initial mutual idealization to the heart wrenching rupture. The roles of Jung, Rank, Groddeck, the members of the “Committee” and others are examined, especially that of Ernest Jones, who pathologized, demonized, and censored Ferenczi's work. In what is one of psychoanalysis's darkest and most dramatic moments, Freud and Jones prevented the publication of Ferenczi's pivotal “Confusion of Tongues,” which Ferenczi had presented at the Wiesbaden Congress in 1932. Ferenczi's innovations and deviations from Freud's theories were interpreted as pathological regression and psychotic deterioration. Rachman, in passionate tone and scholarly detail, sets the record straight. Those close to Ferenczi attested to his clinical genius, success with narcissistic conditions, need for approval by Freud, Freud's rejection, Ferenczi's isolation in Budapest, and his freeing himself from Freud's binding yoke. The circumstances of Ferenczi's death are demystified by Rachman, who argues for the effects of his untreated pernicious anemia and grief over his excommunication by the psychoanalytic establishment. So great was the influence of Freud, Jones, Abraham, and Glover that even Ferenczi's closest students, with the exception of Clara Thompson, publicly disassociated themselves from him for many years.

Peter Giovacchini has devoted his career to finding effective ways to work with patients suffering from pathological narcissism. Modern psychoanalysts and students of modern psychoanalysis will benefit from a careful reading of this book, in which he provides an overview of his life work, and a summative presentation both of his approach to patients and of his principal ideas about narcissism. Modern psychoanalytic readers may find much to challenge or disagree with, but they will also find much that is thought provoking, suggestive, clinically useful, and at certain points convergent with modern psychoanalysis. There is indeed an uneven quality to the book, which may at first challenge the reader's desire to persevere. It contains some autobiographical material, which helps situate the author's developing views about narcissism within a context of clinical experience, which he then attempts to place within a broader cultural and historical framework. It contains some very strong criticism of some of the innovations in psychoanalytic theory and practice, which have been developed to address the difficulties of treating narcissistic patients.

Antisocial Behavior: Personality Disorders From Hostility to Homicide. Benjamin B. Wolman. New York: Prometheus Books, 1999. 211 pp.

Frances Bigda-Peyton EDD

Frances Bigda-Peyton

Frances Bigda-Peyton   Psychoanalysis in Brookline and Bedford, MA. She is field work coordinator for the Institute for the Study of Violence, a division of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis.

Wolman's far-reaching Antisocial Behavior, written for the lay person but applicable to more sophisticated readers as well, examines the rise of sociopathy in modern society. His analysis and ideas about prevention approaches are clear-cut and bold. It is the sort of book one would

281

expect to see from one of the grandfathers of psychoanalysis and founder of the International Journal of Group Tensions.

One disturbing analysis Wolman undertakes is to demonstrate a link between the permissiveness of liberal governments, the historic rise of dictatorships, and the destruction of democratic systems. He documents how in several instances, perceived weakness invited aggression. Wolman acknowledges that the social philosopher Edmund Burke arrived at a similar conclusion 200 years ago: “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.” Wolman sees society as fostering sociopathy by not having strict moral standards that are backed by consistent media messages (especially in relation to violence and selfishness), by tolerating unethical behavior, and by not offering consistent protection to peaceful citizens. He draws examples from many areas, such as international responses to terrorism and our judicial system, which can be permissive and inconsistent.

Wolman carries his argument down to the familial level. Where there is a decline in parental authority, guidance, and discipline, there is the potential for violence and sociopathy. In particular, two kinds of family settings breed sociopathy: slums and broken homes, where there are no clear limits and inadequate role models; and wealthy families, where children are bribed instead of guided and not given meaningful responsibilities. Both environments foster children without self-restraint and without consideration for others. The factors Wolman cites as associated with violence are familiar to all of us: neglect, abuse, lack of supervision, rejection, lack of moral encouragement, physical punishment, inadequate bonding, emotional deprivation and frequent exposure to pathological selfishness.

Even if it were true that before around fourteen months infants are incapable of coding experience in ways that are recoverable in analysis, nonverbal communicative processes of emotional induction or projective identification may play an important role in our work with certain, perhaps even all, of our patients. But it may be an error to assume that such nonverbal processes equate to or derive from primitive preverbal processes and experiences. They may involve subtle and intelligent non-discursive symbolic forms. As analysts working in depth with the unconscious in the here-and-now of the analytic relationship, we recognize our speculations about the past as merely that, and leave the issue of their validity to those who are interested in and capable of conducting scientific research in this field.

This paper presents the case of a girl named Perry. During the four years of treatment, her level of functioning transformed from that of a preverbal child—a crazed, violent, exhausting time for her mother and for me when we never knew from day to day if she would need hospitalization—to that of a person who uses talk as a means for discharging and integrating feelings. The clarity and directness of what she had to say as she finally gave up her primitive, dramatic enactments are a revelation. Since my work with Perry and her mother, who was my original patient, has been so interconnected, the story of the one cannot be told without telling something about the story of the other.

The Object Within: Childbirth as a Developmental Milestone

Lucy Holmes PHD

Lucy Holmes

860 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10021

Lucy Holmes   A psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She also serves as the General Director of the Center for the Advancement of Group Studies. She has served as a Fellow at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and a book reviewer for Modern Psychoanalysis and Modern Group. Currently, she leads groups for women who are dealing with pregnancy, menopause, and adolescent children.

Pregnancy and childbirth can rightly be considered developmental milestones for females, in that they constitute a crisis in the life cycle out of which, in favorable circumstances, new psychic structures are created and mental functioning is integrated. Using the techniques of modem psychoanalytic research, the author discusses themes and unconscious associations regarding childbirth, gathered from data from work with two groups of pregnant women over a period of two years. The complexity of the female endopsychic world is emphasized. Specifically, pregnancy can facilitate a restructuring of the psychic triangle of internalized maternal and paternal objects and self in a way that has a maturational effect. The self gains new authority in relationship to these internalized objects. Existing psychoanalytic literature on childbirth is reviewed, followed by the presentation of a case of a pregnant woman that demonstrates exactly how issues of “masculine” and “feminine” identification become truly integrated in pregnancy and childbirth.

The Internal Triangle: New Theories of Female Development

Lucy Holmes PHD

Lucy Holmes

52 East 78th Street
New York, NY 10021

Lucy Holmes   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City where she also leads groups for women dealing with pregnancy, menopause, and adolescent children. She serves as General Director of the Center for the Advancement of Group Studies.

The internal triangle of maternal imago, paternal imago, and self is unique to female development. Girls are “organless,” and because they can neither suckle their mothers nor penetrate their fathers, they gain control by introjecting both parental objects. The introjection of the preoedipal mother is a primitive incorporation, an oral pre-identification in which mother is ingested with her milk. The internalization of the oedipal father is more highly evolved, a relationship to, as well as a mental representation of, the object. Within the complex endopsychic feminine world, girls freely discharge both libido and aggression toward internalized objects.

This child patient engaged in diverse enactments throughout treatment. Identifying the unconscious conflicts underlying these was complicated due to the preverbal nature of the material and the overlay of multiple traumas that influenced the language and content of her communications. Her impulsivity appeared associated with constitutional preferences for intense motoric forms of discharge. In the transference, she revealed concerns about physical survival and the capacity to breathe. Two dominant conflicts were revealed through her activity: ambivalence about dependency and ambivalence about damaging impulses. Through activity. she also defended against psychic disintegration, sought an experience of bodily containment, and partially satisfied annihilistic urges. Comments about using countertranference when bombarded by dreadful enactments are included.
